2. The petitioners contested the said application before the Labour Court and filed a written statement contending inter alia that the petitioners had been dismissed law fully after holding a fair and proper enquiry into an allegation against them and that that there had been no violation of the principles of natural justice. The learned Labour Court as regards the holding of enquiry into the charges against the respondents found that the enquiry was not fair and proper. He, however, entered into the merits of the allegations against the respondents upon evidence adduced before him on consideration of the evidence in respect of negligence, the Labour Court found that the impugned order of dismissal of the petitioners was not legal and just. The learned Labour Court inter alia held that a single act of negligence as alleged by the petitioner did not constitute misconduct and that in order to constitute misconduct neglect of work should be habitual. The learned Labour Court in this respect held as follows: 

 "Hence it is my opinion and view that mere single neglect of work is not a misconduct and in order to constitute misconduct "neglect" also should be habitual. In the instant cases of fade the charge is for negligence of duty and not for neglect of duty as it will appear from the reading of the charge-sheet and the order of dismissal dated 21.3.75. But it is a charge of negligence of work or neglect of work, it is sure that it is not a charge for habitual negligence of work or habitual neglect of work. There is no evidence either in the enquiry or in the Court proving first parties habitual negligence in work or their habitual neglect of work". 

 Mr. A. R. Yusuf with Mr. Akhtar Imam, Learned Advocate have appeared in support of the rule and Mr. Abu Sufian, learned Advocate appeared to oppose the rule. Mr. A. R. Yusuf, the learned Advocate has submitted that the learned Labour Court misconstrued and misapplied the provisions of clause (h) of sub-section (3) of section 17 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, and has committed an error on the face of the record in flowing that a single act of neglect would not constitute a misconduct and that in order to constitute a misconduct there must be habitual or several acts of neglect of work. He has submitted that whether a single act of neglect would constitute a misconduct or not would vary from the nature of the neglect of work and that a particular work of neglect which may result in accident or endanger the safety of the property of employer may constitute a misconduct He has also submitted that plying of the vessels by a wrong route and running aground the vessels constituted a serious misconduct and in the facts and circumstances of the case the respondents have been rightly dismissed from service. 

 5. As regards the first contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that even a single act of neglect may amount to a misconduct if it is of such a serious nature that it would result in an accident or endanger the safety of the property of the employer, it appears from the evidence considered and found by the learned Labour Court that the accident took place at 10 p.m. on first of March. 1975 and there was a high tide and fog when the flat and the tug ran aground. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to us the certificates of survey of the vessels in question wherein it is seen that the vessels were permitted to ply only at day and not at night in smooth waters. Admittedly there was fog and high tide at the time when the vessels ran aground. The vessel was plying on its way to Barisal. 

 6. In this state of findings and evidence the plying of the launch and the flat in that hour of night and in foggy conditions of the weather must be held to be an act of neglect of work. Now whether this single act of neglect would constitute a misconduct. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that this single act of neglect is of such a serious nature that it has resulted in an accident in running the tug and the flat aground containing valuable oil of a shipper and damaging the property of the employer. We agree with the views of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that whether an act of neglect amounts to misconduct or not depends upon the nature of neglect of work or the seriousness of the act. If an employee commits a particular act which might have resulted in an accident or in damage or in-jury to the goods and property of the employer then it cannot be said that this single act of neglect would not amount to a misconduct under Employment of Labour (Standing Orders Act. In terms of the conditions of the survey certificate issued by the Marine Department of the Government  these vessels were not to ply at night but in violation of the conditions of certificate these vessels plied at night in a foggy condition resulting, in a grounding of the tug and the flat. It will be unconscionable and illogical to say that to constitute a misconduct the employee must have committed several acts of negligence in plying the vessels which might have caused accident or endangered the safety of the vessels if the omission and negligence of the employee is of serious nature then such a single work of neglect would constitute a misconduct. In this connection, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to some decisions in support of his contention that a single act of neglect of work or action or mistake of a serious nature which might have resulted in an accident would constitute or amount to misconduct under clause (h) of sub-section 3 of section 17 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act. The decisions cited by him are reported in AIR 1963 (SC) 1756 and AIR 1957 (SC) 326. He has also pointed out to a decision of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR page 149 wherein it has been held that a single act of neglect of work would not constitute or amount to a misconduct in that the word habitual negligence would also govern the word neglect of work. We are of the view that the facts of that case are not applicable to the case before us. In view of the above discussions, we hold that the aforesaid single act of neglect in plying the vessel during the night and in a foggy condition of weather amounted to a misconduct under clause (h) of sub-section (3) of section 17 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act.
